item.title: Infections are causing cancer, finds new research
item.description: Just five pathogens, including HPV, were found to be the main causes.
item.content:encoded:
Around 12% of the world’s total cancer cases in 2024 were likely caused by an infection, according to new research from the World Health Organization.

The study, published today in The Lancet Oncology, analysed the frequency and causes of different cancers, specifically examining the role of infections.

It linked 2.3 million new cancer cases to an infection. Most were caused by just five pathogens: Helicobacter pylori (4%), human papillomavirus, or HPV (4%), hepatitis B (2%), Epstein-Barr virus (1%) and hepatitis C (under 1%). These infections can cause more than 20 different types of cancer, including stomach, liver, blood and cervical cancers.

So, how can an infection cause cancer? And does this mean these cancers are preventable?

Did we already know about this link?

Some of the study authors have been researching this field for around thirty years. Their previous work investigated cancer cases caused by infections in 1990, 2002, 2008, 2012, and 2018.

The proportion of cancer cases caused by infections may appear to have dropped during those years (from a high of 18% in 2002), but the authors stress these comparisons cannot really be made confidently, as the sources and quality of the data have changed over time.

item.title: ‘Before I Forget’: A touching and surprisingly funny memoir on caring for ageing abusive parents
item.description: In writing about trauma, French writer Anne Pauly is also acerbically funny and no one is spared from her arch humour.
item.content:encoded:
How do you mourn an abusive alcoholic parent? French writer Anne Pauly’s Before I Forget, translated by Dina Leifer, addresses this question in a deeply personal account of grief.

We accompany Pauly’s protagonist and narrator, Anne, as she cares for her ailing father, looking after his house and his personal grooming. Having grown up witnessing her father’s recurrent violence towards her mother, Pauly addresses some very serious topics. She expresses anger towards people who cannot understand why victims of domestic abuse don’t simply leave, saying:

“I’d like to see you, on a Sunday evening, your eye black and blue and your nightshirt torn, hurriedly pack a case for a strip-lit emergency refuge. I’d like to see you, bombarded by insults and threats, find the energy to run to the station with your children and get on a train, not knowing whether you can ever come back.”

In the present, this giant who would chase Anne’s mother around the kitchen table or lock his family out of their home in a drunken rage has been reduced to a sunken form in a wheelchair. These two versions of him co-exist in the narrative.

item.title: Maharashtra’s recognition of women farmers will break gender barriers
item.description: Women Farmers Certificates will recognise women engaged in agriculture or allied activities as farmers, even when they do not own the land.
item.content:encoded:
On October 2, Maharashtra is set to begin issuing the Women Farmers Certificates under the newly enacted Women Farmer’s Empowerment Act 2026. The certificates will formally recognise women engaged in agriculture or allied activities as farmers, even when they do not own the land.

The Women Farmers Certificates will open doors for lakhs of women who sow, tend, harvest and manage our agri-foods systems, as well as livestock, poultry and fisheries, but are often left out of the formal definition of a farmer. Maharashtra has shown political will and a clear sense of urgency in bringing women farmers’ needs into the spotlight and leading by example.

Feminisation of agriculture

We have been witnessing feminisation of agriculture for some time now. As men move to non-farm jobs, women have increasingly taken up the role of managing and maintaining the agricultural lands.

But this has often meant more responsibility without a corresponding rise in control, assets or decision-making power. Without land titles, they also struggle to access critical resources such as credit, water, technology and extension services, reducing them to labourers in a sector they largely sustain.

item.title: Sunday book pick: A tale of a resentful housewife in Shashi Deshpande’s novel ‘That Long Silence’
item.description: Published in 1988, Deshpande’s book received the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1990.
item.content:encoded:
“I had often found family life unendurable. Worse than anything else had been the boredom of the unchanging pattern, the unending monotony. I remember now how often I had sighed for a catastrophe, a disaster, no, not a personal one, but anything to shake us out of our dull grooves.”

Jaya, in Shashi Deshpande’s 1988 novel That Long Silence, is a rare Indian housewife – she hates the dullness of “family life” and the utter boredom of domestic chores. Being needed by her family does not make her proud; in fact, she resents being seen as just the wife and the mother, forever at the beck and call of her moody husband and children.

The novel begins with a “catastrophe”. It is indicated that Jaya’s husband, Mohan, a public works engineer, is hiding from work. It is humiliating for a respectable family such as theirs, so they temporarily shift to their Dadar flat from their Churchgate house. Their teenage children, Rati and Rahul, show the usual boorishness of their age. Jaya despises having Mohan in the flat all day, especially in a sullen mood. item.title: ‘Beyond Our Births’: A debut novel questions the validity of a person’s identity markers
item.description: Antara Mukherjee’s novel is a meditation on love – of its undefined, inexplicable nature, and its borderless provenance.
item.content:encoded:
Beyond Our Births, Antara Mukherjee’s debut novel, is an exploration of the location of identity. Its narrative – that of a child abandoned by her Bangladeshi Muslim parents, adopted by a West Bengali Hindu family, forced to leave when the family’s fortunes turn, accompanied back to Bangladesh by her parents, only to escape from them soon after – continually questions the validity of our identity markers: caste, class, religion, nationality, gender; and underlines their intersectionality in our daily lives.

But the novel is perhaps even more a meditation on love – of its undefined, inexplicable nature, and its borderless provenance: for neither bloodlines nor boundaries between nations, or that between the human and animal can contain it. Nimki, the protagonist of the novel, whom we see grow from five to 15, feels the greatest kinship with Bagha – the family dog of the Senguptas, with whom she lives in Kolkata. “Their lack of language”, we are told, “made them understand each other. They could neither hurt nor delve deep, but heal each other nevertheless with their faithful empathy.”

Nimki needed this empathy as compensation for her perpetual hunger for love in a household that gave her shelter but couldn’t instil a sense of belonging....

item.title: How Modi put Delhi under siege to protect Gyanesh Kumar
item.description: Barricades, tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel as well as right-wing goons were deployed to stop the protests against vote rigging.
item.content:encoded:
What does authoritarianism sound like?

In Delhi’s posh Connaught Place on Saturday, it was the drone of automated police announcements, broadcast on loop from loudspeakers fitted on spiked poles.

“Making groups, taking out marches or any other action is barred,” a robotic voice announced. “Everyone should peacefully move out from here and follow the police’s orders.”

A few feet away, the intersection bristled with paramilitary troops waiting to pounce on any protester they could spot. On the other side was a wall of yellow barricades. The street was empty. The Delhi Police had blocked off almost all traffic to Connaught Place, the city centre.

This unprecedented bandobast was intended to stop demonstration against Gyanesh Kumar, India’s Chief Election Commissioner, who protestors allege has rigged the voter rolls to favour the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party.

On Saturday, the Modi government pulled out all stops to protect Kumar.

The fort of Delhi

To prevent protesters from reaching Jantar Mantar, a legally designated protest site a few hundred metres from Connaught Place, the Delhi Police cordoned off the city centre with several layers of barricades. It also shut down all metro stations in the area. item.title: TM Krishna: For generations, ‘Hum Dekhenge’ has stripped the cloak off powerful narcissists
item.description: In Iqbal Bano’s rendition, a song of protest that seeks to unsettle the powerful and foretells their downfall is cased in a delicate, poised melody.
item.content:encoded:
As protesters all over India demand the resignation of the chief election commissioner and the restoration of every citizen’s voting rights, I offer this musical note of solidarity.

For generations, Faiz Ahmed Faiz’s Hum Dekhenge has been an integral part of protests, a metaphor for resistance, justice and democracy, and since 2019 it has seeped into our wider national consciousness. While its history and lyrical depth is well known, the song’s musical cadence is less discussed. The gold standard for this song is without doubt the rendition by Iqbal Bano in her stirring protest against Zia-ul-Haq, and that is the basis of this piece.

Hum Dekhenge is not an activist’s chanting song, shrill in tonality, fast in tempo, with an un-decorative melody. It is simple, yet nuanced in its flow and melodic direction. Iqbal Bano’s rendition is unusually slow, embedded with filigree work and subtle movements that allow the song to unfold evocatively.

The way Bano renders Woh din ke jiskaa vaada hai, with jiskaa meandering ever so slightly, followed by a stunning musical drop at vaada hai leading sharply to hum dekhenge is stunning. She follows that up with a tantalising glide across the octave, sensuously singing the phrase jo lauh-e-azal me likha hai.

item.title: UN flags CEC protest mass detentions, says curbs must meet ‘necessity and proportionality’ tests
item.description: New Delhi rejected the concerns and accused the UN body of having an ‘approach of extreme selectivity’ and ‘double standards’ regarding public positions.
item.content:encoded:
The United Nations Human Rights Office on Saturday expressed concern over the mass detention of protesters in Delhi during demonstrations demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation, saying restrictions on peaceful protests “must meet strict tests of necessity and proportionality”.

The UN body called for the immediate and unconditional release of those arbitrarily detained.

India rejected the concerns, describing them as “misplaced” and “an unwarranted interference in the internal affairs of India”.

The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights called on the Indian authorities to respect the right to peaceful assembly.

It said that it was “concerned by reports of mass detentions of demonstrators, protest leaders, members of civil society organisations, lawyers and journalists, before and during today’s large-scale demonstrations in Delhi”.

UN Human Rights spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan urged the authorities to engage in “meaningful dialogue” to address the concerns raised by protesters.

Responding to the remarks, the Ministry of External Affairs accused the UN body of having an “approach of extreme selectivity” regarding public positions.

“Violent responses to protests in our neighbourhood have gone uncommented, as indeed have law enforcement actions in its own vicinity,” the ministry said. “Such double standards only erode the credibility of its standing and contribute to the loss of faith in multilateralism.”

item.title: ‘Darkness and Other Stories’: A collection of Razia Sajjad Zaheer’s politically conscious fiction
item.description: This collection, translated from the Urdu by Saba Mahmood Bashir, will appeal to scholars of gender studies, Partition studies, and postcolonial literature.
item.content:encoded:
In the short story “Darkness,” from the collection Darkness and Other Stories – translated from the Urdu by Saba Mahmood Bashir – Razia Sajjad Zaheer describes a train journey whose anxieties are all too familiar to Muslims today. The protagonist is Zaheer herself, who has boarded her train at the Old Delhi Railway Station and is headed for Amritsar.

We are reminded of Rasheed Jahan, another fiery progressive writer, whose “Dilli ki Sair” had chalked out a different struggle – a woman who must idly wait at the Delhi railway station amidst strange men, a stand-by object like the luggage itself, while her husband struts about with an old friend. But Zaheer is not bound to any consort. She is a university graduate, she is a progressive writer of Urdu fiction; she also happens to be a Muslim woman.

As the story progresses, there is a feverish fear that slowly grips her; there is no other woman in her First-Class coach, and Zaheer’s Muslim name is hanging on the coupe, a bright red mark of her vulnerability. item.title: ‘A focus on literature that is part of everyday life’: Onaiza Drabu on editing a Kashmiri anthology
item.description: An interview with the editor of ‘The Big Book of Kashmiri Literature’.
item.content:encoded:
“I wanted to make the case for the fact that literature is everywhere; it is omnipresent.”

That is what Onaiza Drabu aimed to do with The Big Book of Kashmiri Literature, the anthology she has edited that illustrates the richness of Kashmiri literature, land, and people through a diverse canon of expressions.

The anthology brings together the works of several historical saints, scholars, unlettered poets, and voices of Kashmir, ranging from the fourteenth century to the contemporary era.

In a conversation with Scroll, Drabu spoke about the making of The Big Book of Kashmiri Literature, the inspiration for the project, the process of collecting literary works from earlier centuries and selecting texts for an anthology of this scale.

item.title: How TV channels covered the protests as ‘anarchy’ and ignored the detentions of journalists
item.description: The police allowed mainstream television channels to broadcast from Central Delhi while restricting access for several reporters from independent media.
item.content:encoded:
Around 4.30 pm on Saturday, Republic TV, the news channel helmed by Arnab Goswami, flashed this headline on television screens across the country: “CJP Flop Show”.

It referred to the protests in Delhi, called by the Cockroach Janta Party and Left student outfits, against the special intensive revision of voter lists – a controversial exercise that has disenfranchised millions, driving many Indians to take to the streets and demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

By the time Republic TV flashed that headline, credible reports about the police having detained over a dozen journalists for simply reporting on the protests, including three from Scroll, had been in circulation for hours. Many of these journalists were detained while they were documenting how the police were clamping down on protesters.

The high-handedness of the authorities, even towards fellow members of the press, found no mention in Republic TV’s coverage. The same broadly held true for other Hindi and English television news channels as well. Their reporters and anchors limited themselves to broadcasting the police and the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party’s point of view on the protests for most of Saturday.

item.title: The Ghanian scholar who changed how the world hears African music
item.description: Kofi Agawu challenged the idea that African music is something that is ‘felt’ rather than thought about analytically.
item.content:encoded:
Kofi Agawu is regarded as one of the world’s foremost authorities on African music. The Ghanaian scholar, teacher and researcher has changed how the world hears and studies it.

I am a scholar of indigenous African music. I have researched and written extensively on African indigenous knowledge systems and worldviews.

I also know Professor Agawu personally. He has visited my institution, the University of Venda in South Africa. In this article, I pay tribute to his pioneering work in African musicology while taking issue with one finer point in his theories. This, I think, makes for a more useful tribute than unbroken praise.

The invention of African rhythm

Kofi Agawu, who turns 70 on 28 September 2026, was born in Hohoe in Ghana’s Volta region. He is Ewe, which is the dominant group of the region. He finished school at Achimota in Accra, studied in Britain and completed a doctorate at Stanford University in 1982. After many years at Princeton, he now teaches at the City University of New York Graduate Center.

Across six books he has made it very hard to go on saying that African music is something that is “felt” rather than something that is thought about analytically.

item.title: Lessons for the 21st century from Mary Shelley’s 1826 novel ‘The Last Man’
item.description: Set in the late 21st century, the novel is about a lethal contagion spread by human conflict that sweeps the world and seemingly leaves one sole human survivor.
item.content:encoded:
Even if you have never read it, you know the story of Mary Shelley’s second great work of political science fiction after Frankenstein. The Last Man, published in 1826 but set in the late 21st century, tells the tale of a lethal contagion spread by human conflict and war that sweeps the world and seemingly leaves one sole human survivor.

With wars and climate catastrophes hitting a world still reeling from 7 million deaths caused by Covid-19, Shelley’s pandemic novel has perhaps never felt so relevant.

And the book’s influence is widespread. The tropes and themes of The Last Man have shaped the genre of postapocalyptic fiction in the two centuries since its release. In Shelley’s Frankenstein and the many stories, films and TV shows it has inspired, the abandoned monster becomes a plague upon his creator.

In The Last Man and the countless books and movies on its themes that followed, a human-made epidemic becomes the mega-monster that threatens the extinction of humanity itself.

Some of the recent television series that explore these themes are The Last of Us, Midnight Mass, and Station Eleven. They follow classic films such as I Am Legend, 28 Days Later, and The Last Man on Earth.

Regardless of how many zombie-invasion or vampire-apocalypse movies you have seen, if you haven’t read The Last Man, I recommend you do. And if you have, perhaps read it again.

Nine persons were killed between Friday and Saturday in Manipur’s Kamjong, Kangpokpi and Ukhrul districts, the Hindustan Times reported, quoting unidentified police officials.

At least 14 homes were burnt in Kamjong and the district authorities have imposed prohibitory orders within a 400-metre radius of Chassad police station.

The violence followed the death of a 42-year-old woman, who was killed in the Kuki-dominated Chassad village in Naga-majority Kamjong district, reported PTI. A mother of five, the woman was shot near her neck on Friday night during a gunfight between armed groups and security forces.

The gunfight had started after security forces arrested some village volunteers, reported Hindustan Times.

The term “village volunteers” has been used for armed civilians guarding villages since ethnic clashes broke out in the state between the Kuki and Meitei groups in May 2023.

The women’s death on Friday triggered an exchange of fire between Kuki and Naga armed groups, reported PTI. A 22-year-old man was killed in the clashes and at least 14 homes belonging to members of the Kuki and Naga communities were burnt.

Separately, suspected militants opened fire in the Ningchou village, a Tangkhul Naga settlement near the Myanmar border, in Kamjong, reported PTI.

Sometimes, I like to pick up a book without reading anything about it first. Sometimes, it is just the blurb, or perhaps only the title. Nothing else. Sometimes, the fact that a translator decided to translate a certain novel is enough. I find it satisfying to let a story tell itself on its own terms. I’m willingly led by it – I do not try to anticipate where it is headed. Urdu writer Mohsin Khan’s novel Allah Miyan’s Workshop, translated by Maaz Bin Bilal, turned out to be one such book for me. I picked it up knowing almost nothing about it, and perhaps that was the best way to read it.

A child’s world

The novel’s central character is Gibran, a curious 14-year-old boy living in Awadh. item.title: ‘Grief Burns Like Fever’: This novel is a flashback of depravity during the surreal pandemic years
item.description: Minakshi Thakur’s book spans every economic stratum of our society and how each responded to this unforeseen, dystopian situation.
item.content:encoded:
It is hard to find anything we’d all collectively agree or disagree with, but if there’s one thing that unites Indians is our vehement determination to repress and suppress all and every memory of the dreadful Covid-19 pandemic years.

Today, those three odd years seem like a hazy dream, a delirium where nothing and no one resembled what they once were, and it is not surprising that so many of us have retained virtually no memories of the time.

Every hour of every day was the same; the world was cut off, we were cooped up inside our homes – this would not have been so bad, and could have even been tolerated as a painfully prolonged and mandatory family-bonding exercise if not for infected air and the piling up of the dead.

Little islands

item.title: How the French convinced Indian workers to stay on in the Caribbean despite systemic abuse
item.description: After slavery was abolished, Indian workers became vital to Guadeloupe’s sugar economy. When their contracts ended, colonisers tried to make them stay.
item.content:encoded:
When the Nantes-Bordeaux steamship left Indian waters and set sail for the French Caribbean in November 1888, it carried 597 men, women and children from Calcutta, Pondicherry, and Karaikal, all hoping to escape poverty by working for a few years in Guadeloupe.

The voyage quickly turned into an ordeal. After the ship broke down near Cape Guardafui, the passengers were stranded aboard at the port of Aden for a month while repairs were carried out. During the delay, many suffered from scurvy, a disease caused by vitamin C deficiency. By the time the ship reached Guadeloupe, four infants, two women and one man had died on board. Two men, apparently frustrated by the ordeal, jumped overboard.

The difficulties they faced during the voyage, however, were only part of the story.

French colonisers in the Caribbean had begun recruiting Indian indentured workers from the Madras Presidency, Pondicherry, Karaikal and Calcutta to address severe labour shortages on sugar plantations after the abolition of slavery in 1848. Many of the workers aboard the Nantes-Bordeaux had already lived in places such as Guadeloupe and Martinique and had chosen to return to the Caribbean because life in India presented its own economic and social hardships.

item.title: Wave of protests shows that Indian democracy’s greatest strength is its ‘million mutinies’
item.description: Just as when VS Naipaul wrote those words, today’s upheavals will transform India.
item.content:encoded:
In 1990, when VS Naipaul published India: A Million Mutinies Now, he gave India a phrase that has acquired an almost prophetic resonance: “a country of a million little mutinies.”

He was not predicting a revolution. He was describing something more consequential – the awakening of the individual.

Naipaul had returned to a country that had changed dramatically since his earlier, far darker journeys through India. He saw people emerging from the inherited certainties of caste, class, family, religion, region and tradition, demanding that they be allowed to decide for themselves who they were and what their lives ought to mean.

Emergence from dominant political thoughts was part of this process. His most important insight was that freedom does not necessarily arrive looking orderly.

“Independence was worked for by people more or less at the top; the freedom it brought has worked its way down,” he wrote. And then came the crucial observation: “People everywhere have ideas now of who they are and what they owe themselves.”

That is the heart of Naipaul’s argument.

Freedom creates expectations. Expectations create demands. Demands create friction. And friction creates protest. They came from a wide range of backgrounds: plumbers as well as politicians, instrument-makers as well as monarchs, women and immigrants alongside aristocrats and merchants; playwrights, poets and artists, too. They were a tiny minority but their wealth, their power and their appetite for risk influenced not just Britain’s economy but its politics, science, arts and institutions – from the development of the Royal Navy and the restoration of the Stuart monarchy to the emergence of two-party politics, the free press and Parliament itself.

Drawing on a years-long project to unearth the identities of 13,000 individual investors, Britain's Slave Traders shows not only how they helped win wars, shape modern industry and make Britain the global and imperial force it eventually became, but how their drive to open up the trade contributed to Britain’s reputation as a freedom-loving nation and how slavery’s profits improved the lives of the neediest Britons through hospitals, almshouses and schools.

Britain’s Slave Traders corrects a profound distortion of the past, revealing a previously obscured but vital thread within Britain’s history.

The Malayalam film turns the police procedural on its head, borrowing a few ideas from Drishyam to craft a cat-and-mouse game packed with suspense and twists.

An excellent Parvathy Thiruvothu plays Aleena, who forms a tight team with fellow cops Dasan (Sidharth Bharathan), Divya (Unnimaya Prasad) and Sreenath (Mathew Thomas). The nightmare for the quartet begins when a man who has been behaving suspiciously is brought to the police station for questioning. A gun goes off and the man dies.

Which of the four cops fired the gun is the first worry. How the crime is to be covered up is the other. Harris (Vijayaraghavan), a Crime Branch officer with a formidable reputation for sniffing out lies, senses that the story presented by the cops is too iron-clad to be genuine.

When violence broke out in Manipur in 2023, Hoihnu Hauzel was “in a state of disbelief”. Her home was burnt down and her family had to flee to a neighbouring state.

A journalist for the past 15 years, Hauzel said she had not intended to make a record of such a disaster. But then a publication asked her to write a piece.

“…It dawned on me that the only thing I could do was write and not to keep an account, but to document what was unfolding in front of me,” she said.

The result was Stories the Fire Could Not Burn, a personal account of the ethnic conflict that has left more than 300 people dead and close to 60,000 displaced. Her book of poetry, Requiem for a Home in Manipur, is a personal reflection on the loss of home during the prolonged unrest in the state.

item.title: Roadblocks to democracy: What’s really at stake when the state restricts transport services?
item.description: The curbs announced ahead of Saturday’s protest in Delhi show how curtailing movement can be used as an instrument for governing dissent.
item.content:encoded:
For decades, blocking transport has been among the most recognisable tactics of protest politics in India.

Farmers frequently block highways, unions organise chakka jams, and rail roko agitations have a history stretching back to the freedom movement. The logic is straightforward: disrupting everyday circulation makes a political claim harder to ignore. But the inconvenience caused to ordinary travellers is precisely why such tactics have also attracted criticism.

The state, of course, has also restricted movement during protests for a long time. Roads have been barricaded, protest sites cordoned off, and access to cities curtailed in the name of public order. During the 2020-’21 farmers’ protests, Delhi’s borders were fortified by digging ditches, erecting concrete barriers, rolling out razor wire and even installing iron nails into roads.

The farmers were allowed to protest at the Tikri, Singhu, and Ghazipur borders, but their movement toward the institutions in the centre of the capital was constrained.

October 10 therefore is not the first time the state has deployed mobility restrictions. What is striking, though, is their sheer scale. item.title: Russia: ‘Plague’ death is causing panic but there is little reason to worry for now
item.description: The availability of treatment, rapid testing and contact tracing mean the outlook of plague is very different today.
item.content:encoded:
A laboratory worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Siberia, Russia, has died just days after falling ill with an undisclosed illness.

While reports of suspected plague have been circulating in the media, Russia’s consumer health watchdog has described the illness as pneumonia of unknown cause. The World Health Organization also stated the official cause of death has not yet been confirmed. Plague therefore remains only a possible explanation.

While this is a tragic death and an important investigation, it’s certainly not a reason to panic or sign that the Black Death has returned. The availability of treatment, rapid testing and contact tracing mean the outlook of plague is very different today.

Why is plague suspected?

It’s currently not clear what the laboratory technician’s cause of death was. But as the research institute where she worked studies plague bacteria, health authorities are right to consider plague as a potential cause of illness.

The illness that she experienced – a form of pneumonia that ended in her death just a few days of contracting it – also resembles symptoms of pneumonic plague.

item.content:encoded:
The Allahabad High Court on Thursday questioned the use of the term “andolanjeevi” in the grounds for detaining journalist Satyam Verma under the National Security Act after the workers’ protests in Noida, Live Law reported.

“Where did this term ‘andolanjeevi’ come from?” the court was quoted as asking verbally. “How did it find its way into an official document?”

Prime Minister Narendra Modi first used the term in 2021 during protests against the now-repealed farm laws, describing protesters as a new category of people who “are like parasites who feed off protests”.

This might seem like a highly inflammatory statement, but it is true that there are times when infringement of the law becomes a necessity. The aim of law is to ensure that every individual can exercise their freedom and enjoy their rights as a social being, with the tacit corollary that they do not deny another’s right to the same. However, there was a period in Kerala’s history when caste hierarchy and associated norms existed as a law in itself. Caste norms regulated an individual’s life and were enforced via coercion by upper-caste Hindus and implemented through mute and submissive compliance by the Dalits. item.title: Infosys, Tata, Wipro among Indian IT firms suspended from US green card programme

The United States on Thursday suspended information technology companies Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe from the Permanent Labor Certification Programme. The process allows employers to sponsor foreign workers, including H-1B visa holders, for employment-based green cards.

Infosys, Tata, Wipro and HCL are India-based IT firms.

The action does not cancel existing H-1B visas held by employees of these companies. Permanent Labor Certification is a separate process that employers must complete before filing petitions for most employment-based green cards. Under the programme, employers must establish that there are no qualified, willing and available US workers for a particular job.

A green card allows a foreign citizen to live and work permanently in the US. H-1B visas allow companies in the US to temporarily employ foreign workers for special occupations.

The move is part of a broader immigration crackdown under President Donald Trump, whose second term began in January 2025.

On Thursday, US Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said that the Department of Labor would “not accept any new or process any pending Permanent Labor Certification applications” involving the companies.

The Andhra Pradesh government has declared a drought in 21 of its 28 districts as the rainfall deficit from June to August in the state stood at 53%, reported The Hindu on Thursday.

The deficit in rainfall was due to the effects of El Niño, which is a phenomenon that involves the warming of ocean surface temperatures in the eastern and central Pacific. It typically occurs every few years and has been linked to reduced monsoon rainfall in India.

The Kharif season in India is between June and October.

Fifteen years later, the national capital is once again aflame with protests. Will they similarly build up momentum for political change in 2029?

There are strong parallels between 2011 and 2026.

In 2011, after protests in Jantar Mantar in April, Ramlila Maidan saw two rounds of mass demonstrations – the first in June, the second in August.

This year, barely two months after young people took over Jantar Mantar in June, a second wave is building up, with the police this week blocking even Opposition leaders from reaching the protest square.

In 2011, it was about “corruption”. In 2026, it is about “rigging” – of exam papers, of the election system. Almost all her literary production has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning. Carson’s oeuvre across forms and genres comprises more than 30 works. Among her notable works are Autobiography of Red: A Novel in Verse (1998), Norma Jean Baker of Troy: a version of Euripides’ Helen (2019) and translations of Sophocles’s Electra, and of Euripides’s Grief Lessons: Four Plays.

The Delhi Election Commission on Wednesday said that it will organise special camps to ensure that voters whose homes have been demolished recently are not excluded from the special intensive revision of electoral rolls.

This came amid concerns over deletions of names from the electoral rolls during the voter list revision exercise. The interest of the country must be given “paramount consideration”, the bench said. It held that Mustt Hasena Bhanu had failed to provide sufficient documentary evidence to establish her Indian citizenship and her claimed family links, the newspaper reported.

The court was hearing Bhanu’s challenge to a May 19, 2017, order of a foreigners’ tribunal, which had declared her a foreigner who entered India after March 25, 1971.

The tribunal had found that she failed to establish her links to the people she identified as her father and grandfather.

The foreigners tribunals in Assam are quasi-judicial bodies that adjudicate on matters of citizenship based on lineage and a 1971 cut-off date. They rely primarily on documents submitted by persons to establish their family’s residency in Assam or India before 1971.

Those declared foreigners by the tribunals have the option to appeal the decision before the High Court or the Supreme Court.

item.title: Actor Nana Patekar dies at 75

item.content:encoded:
Veteran actor Nana Patekar died at the age of 75 after suffering a cardiac arrest at his home in Goa on Thursday, PTI reported.

Patekar was found unconscious at his apartment early in the morning and was taken to hospital, the news agency quoted the doctor at the medical facility as saying.

A medico-legal case has been registered and a postmortem will be conducted.

item.title: Punjab’s prisons are awash with de-addiction pills. But is that good news?
item.description: The High Court and an assembly panel have flagged the surge in supply to jails. Some experts say this may be a sign of growing addiction.
item.content:encoded:
In 2017, the Punjab government introduced a new therapy for victims of drug abuse.

It involved putting users of opioids like heroin – colloquially called chitta – on a combination of less potent opioids to wean them off their addiction.

The substitute – buprenorphine and naloxone pills – was meant to be taken orally and under medical supervision. According to a psychiatrist who works in one of Punjab’s central jails, the therapy drastically reduced the vulnerability of an addict.

“Firstly, there is no intravenous use because of which an addict is likely to get infected with HIV, hepatitis or other diseases,” he said. “There is almost zero chance of drug overdose death.”

The therapy was rolled out across more than 529 clinics over the years and met with limited success. In November 2023, the Punjab government informed the Assembly that around 80-90% of patients who complete this treatment at the state’s Outpatient Opioid Assisted Treatment clinics relapse into addiction.

Strikingly, in the last four years, the supply of buprenorphine pills to Punjab’s prisons has surged and the number of inmates registered with deaddiction clinics has doubled, the Punjab government’s figures show.

item.title: Maritime history: How merchants transcended caste and faith identity to rule over sea trade
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Indians in the Ocean: Cultures of Trade and Travel ca 1000-1500 CE’, by Mahmood Kooria.
item.content:encoded:
Major maritime merchant communities from the subcontinent transcended religious, regional and caste identities. In the existing literature, they are often identified along these lines, yet such classifications do not fully capture the fluid and interconnected nature of their networks, as in the case of Banias, which included Buddhists and Jains earlier, but also Hindus and even Muslims later. The same goes with Lohanas as well as Klings and Chulias, all who crossed the borders of religions as much as of the regions. It would be impossible to enlist and analyse all mercantile groups from the subcontinent here, but below I provide snapshots of a few major transoceanic communities active between the 11th and 16th centuries.

Until the end of the first millennium in the subcontinent, Buddhist and Jain traders played a major role in the oceanic world, often mirroring their influence in overland commerce. The boundaries between these groups in the maritime mercantile contexts were blurry, but we do see occasional references for them competing for economic and political influence.

item.title: What questions and debates in Parliament say about India’s climate change priorities

India, like other countries, is grappling with the effects of El Niño, which has exacerbated global warming, causing a major rainfall deficit in the country this year. Over the past decade, India has seen climate change take a deadly toll in the form of extreme weather and disasters such as landslides and glacial collapse.

How did these concerns resonate in the Indian Parliament?

In the last 10 years, Parliament maintained a steady focus on climate change, but its attention has centered largely on setting ambitious goals and announcing national targets.

What followed were two years of devastating war waged by the Israel Defense Forces in Gaza, which a United Nations commission of inquiry, leading genocide scholars and major human rights organisations have concluded amounted to genocide. Much of the strip lies in ruins and more than 74,000 Palestinians are dead, with thousands more believed to remain buried under the rubble.

A year ago this week, a US-imposed ceasefire was finally forced on both sides – though mainly on paper. While major IDF assaults have ceased, Israeli attacks in Gaza have continued, in addition to unbridled Jewish settler violence in the West Bank.
